chapter_title: Planning and Design for OpenStack Deployments
chapter_summary:
Designing a Red Hat OpenStack Platform deployment is a complex undertaking that requires meticulous planning to ensure scalability, performance, and security. As an RHCA, your role is to translate business requirements into a robust architectural blueprint. The first critical step is **sizing**. This involves estimating the required compute (CPU, RAM), storage (block, object, file), and networking resources based on anticipated workload demands. Don't just consider the initial deployment; plan for future growth. Factor in oversubscription ratios for CPU and RAM, but be cautious not to over-commit too aggressively, as it can lead to performance degradation. For storage, consider IOPS, throughput, and capacity requirements for different types of workloads (e.g., databases vs. web servers). A common mistake is underestimating the control plane's resource needs; the OpenStack services themselves require significant resources, especially for large deployments or high availability configurations. Always consult Red Hat's reference architectures and sizing guides for best practices.

Next, **networking design** is arguably the most intricate part of an OpenStack deployment. Neutron, the networking service, offers immense flexibility but also complexity. You'll need to define both **provider networks** and **self-service (tenant) networks**. Provider networks are typically mapped directly to physical network infrastructure, offering high performance and simplicity but less flexibility for tenants. Self-service networks, on the other hand, are entirely virtual and managed by tenants, often using overlay technologies like **VXLAN** or **GRE** to encapsulate traffic over an underlay network. While VXLAN provides greater scalability (up to 16 million network segments) compared to VLANs (4096 segments), it introduces overhead and requires proper configuration of the underlay network to handle encapsulated traffic efficiently. A robust design often involves a combination: provider networks for external connectivity and specific high-bandwidth services, and self-service networks for tenant isolation and flexibility. Ensure you plan for dedicated network interfaces for different traffic types (management, API, storage, tenant data) to optimize performance and security.

**Storage considerations** are equally vital. While OpenStack's Cinder and Swift services provide the interfaces, the underlying storage backend dictates performance and reliability. For enterprise-grade RHOSP deployments, **Red Hat Ceph Storage** is the de facto standard. Ceph provides a unified, highly scalable, and fault-tolerant storage solution that can serve as the backend for Cinder (block storage via RBD), Glance (image storage), and Swift (object storage). When designing with Ceph, consider the number of OSDs (Object Storage Daemons), their hardware (SSDs for journals/WAL, spinning disks for data), network bandwidth for Ceph replication, and placement groups. Proper Ceph design ensures high IOPS and throughput, crucial for demanding VM workloads. Failing to adequately plan for storage performance can be a major bottleneck for your cloud.

Finally, integrating **security zones** into your OpenStack design is non-negotiable for an RHCA. This involves segmenting your network and services based on trust levels and sensitivity. For example, the OpenStack control plane (Keystone, Nova API, Neutron API) should reside in a highly secured management zone, isolated from tenant data networks. Tenant workloads themselves can be segmented into different security zones using Neutron's security groups and network policies. Consider firewall rules at the physical network layer and within OpenStack to enforce traffic flow policies. When using TripleO, the deployment process itself enforces many security best practices, but architects must ensure the overall design aligns with organizational security policies. This includes planning for network segmentation, strong authentication mechanisms (e.g., integrating Keystone with LDAP or IdM), and ensuring all components are deployed with the principle of least privilege. Neglecting security at the design phase often leads to costly retrofits or, worse, security breaches.

screens.title: Planning and Design for OpenStack Deployments
screens.subtitle: Sizing, networking, storage, and security considerations for RHOSP

narration.text: As an architect you translate business needs into a resilient OpenStack blueprint. This lesson will show you how to size compute, storage, and network resources, choose appropriate network topologies and encapsulation, evaluate Red Hat Ceph Storage for different workloads, and integrate security zones so services and tenant workloads remain properly isolated. We will emphasize practical trade-offs: when to use provider networks for high performance and when to rely on self-service overlay networks for tenant flexibility. For storage, we'll examine how Ceph acts as a unified backend for block, object, and image services and what hardware and network design choices drive IOPS and latency. Finally, we’ll discuss how the control plane must be treated as a first-class resource and how TripleO influences secure deployment patterns. Throughout, expect concrete examples you can use in capacity planning, a small lab-style network design exercise, and common pitfalls to avoid. By the end you will be able to produce a deployment sketch that balances performance, scalability, and security for an enterprise OpenStack cloud.

keyIdea.title: Core design focus
keyIdea.text: Balance sizing, network architecture, storage backend design, and security zoning to deliver a scalable, performant OpenStack deployment.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to design and evaluate

narration.text: These objectives focus your design work and testing. First, you will develop a comprehensive sizing strategy for compute, storage, and networking. That means estimating C P U and R A M for VMs, planning oversubscription ratios carefully, and allocating adequate control plane resources. A concrete example is sizing Nova and the database services for a high-availability deployment rather than relying only on VM estimates. Second, you will design network topologies that distinguish provider and self-service networks and choose appropriate encapsulation methods such as VLAN or VXLAN. You should be able to justify using a provider network for high-bandwidth services and VXLAN for large multi-tenant scale. Third, you will evaluate storage backend options, with emphasis on Red Hat Ceph Storage, and map IOPS, throughput, and placement group choices to workload needs. Finally, you will formulate security zone strategies that isolate the control plane, storage, and tenant traffic, integrate Keystone with enterprise identity, and apply least-privilege policies. Each objective pairs a practical deliverable with a reason why it reduces deployment risk.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Learning Objectives
Deliverables you will produce
  • Sizing table: CPU, RAM, disk IOPS, and control-plane reserve for a pilot and projected growth.
  • Network sketch: Provider interface mappings and tenant overlay design showing encapsulation choice.
  • Ceph layout: OSD count, journal strategy, public/cluster networks, and placement group guidance.
  • Security policy map: Zones for management, API, storage, and tenant workloads with integration notes for identity.
Assessment hint
Use a small pilot to validate your assumptions. Plans should be defensible to operations and security teams.
Mnemonic & example
Example: For a database VM class, specify CPU cores, RAM, expected IOPS, and map to a Ceph pool with SSD-backed OSDs. Note the control plane needs additional RAM and CPU beyond per-VM totals to remain responsive.
Common misconception
A common mistake is sizing based only on initial VM counts without reserving capacity for controllers, orchestration tasks, and bursts. Always include a stability margin.

screens.title: Sizing: Principles and Control Plane
screens.subtitle: Estimate compute and reserve for the OpenStack control plane

narration.text: Sizing begins with clear definitions of your workload classes and the control plane. Define VM classes by expected C P U, R A M, disk, and IOPS. For each class, estimate average and peak resource use. Then consider the control plane — services like Keystone, Nova scheduler, placement, Cinder, Glance, message queues and the database. These services require dedicated capacity, especially in high-availability setups where multiple active controllers are used. A concrete example: a small production deployment with 200 VMs may require multiple controller nodes with extra C P U and memory reserved for message queues and A P I processing, not just the sum of guest VM requirements. Oversubscription ratios for C P U and R A M are useful but must be conservative; 4:1 C P U oversubscription may work for general-purpose workloads but will harm latency-sensitive applications. Always plan a safety margin for spikes from operations tasks such as live migration, backups, and image imports. A common misconception is to treat controller services as lightweight — in medium and large clouds they can consume substantial resources. Key takeaway: separate per-VM capacity calculations from control plane reserves and validate with a pilot to avoid surprise contention.

keyIdea.title: Control plane matters
keyIdea.text: Reserve separate capacity for OpenStack services; do not fold control plane requirements into VM totals.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Sizing: Principles
Definition & claim
Sizing is the estimation of CPU, RAM, storage IOPS/throughput, and network capacity for both tenant workloads and the OpenStack control plane. It must account for current needs and projected growth.
Step: classify workloads
Create VM classes (web, app, DB) with typical CPU/RAM and IOPS.
Step: reserve control plane
Allocate separate nodes/cores and memory for services like Keystone, Nova, Glance, RabbitMQ, and the DB.
Step: plan oversubscription
Choose conservative CPU/RAM oversubscription ratios and validate with load tests.
Key Takeaway

Never treat control plane services as negligible; allocate dedicated capacity and include operational spikes in your calculations.

Concrete example
A pilot with 200 general-purpose VMs might calculate per-VM resources then add 3 controller nodes each with extra CPU and RAM for message queues, databases, and API load. Plan for migration and backup spikes.
Common mistake
Counting only VM consumption and omitting control plane headroom. This causes API slowness and scheduler stalls under load.
Quick checklist
  • Define VM classes and peaks.
  • Reserve capacity for controllers.
  • Choose conservative oversubscription.
  • Run pilot tests to validate.

screens.title: Storage Sizing and Workload Characteristics
screens.subtitle: Match IOPS, throughput, and capacity to workload types

narration.text: Storage sizing requires mapping workload characteristics to backend capabilities. Start by classifying workloads: transactional databases need high IOPS and low latency, while web servers require more capacity and modest throughput. For each category record expected IOPS per VM, average and peak throughput, and capacity needs. Translate these numbers to Ceph design parameters: the number and type of OSDs, whether to use SSDs for journals or WAL, and how many placement groups to configure. For example, a database pool could use SSD-backed OSDs or dedicated SSD devices for journals to improve latency. Also consider replication or erasure coding selection: replication is simpler and often better for small-block IOPS-heavy workloads, while erasure coding can save capacity for large object stores with less frequent small writes. A frequent mistake is to size only for capacity and ignore IOPS and network bandwidth; Ceph performance is closely tied to network throughput, so provision a dedicated high-bandwidth network for replication. Key takeaway: design storage by workload profile and validate through load testing to reveal bottlenecks before wide-scale deployment. Storage Sizing and Workload Characteristics means design ceph topology around iops and latency for demanding workloads; capacity alone is insufficient.. In practical terms, match iops, throughput, and capacity to workload types. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: IOPS first
keyIdea.text: Design Ceph topology around IOPS and latency for demanding workloads; capacity alone is insufficient.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Storage Sizing
Process steps
  1. Classify workloads by IOPS, latency, and capacity.
  2. Map workload class to Ceph pool type and OSD hardware.
  3. Decide replication factor or erasure coding policy.
  4. Plan network bandwidth for Ceph public and cluster traffic.
  5. Validate with synthetic and real workload testing.
Key Takeaway
Match Ceph hardware and network design to the IOPS and latency needs of your critical workloads, not only to capacity targets.
Concrete scenario
A transactional database pool: choose SSD-backed OSDs or use SSDs for WAL/journals, set a replication factor of three, and ensure a dedicated 10GbE or higher network for Ceph replication to avoid contention with tenant traffic.
Misconception
Assuming that more storage disks alone will fix latency. Without appropriate OSD hardware and network bandwidth, adding disks can increase variance and worsen performance.
Example layout
<-- Ceph OSD plan -->
OSD devices: mix of NVMe/SSD for WAL, HDD for bulk data
Replication: 3
Placement groups: sized to OSD count for even distribution
Networks: separate public and cluster networks; high bandwidth

screens.title: Red Hat Ceph Storage Design Considerations
screens.subtitle: OSDs, journals, placement groups, and network bandwidth

narration.text: Designing Ceph for RHOSP requires decisions about OSD count, device roles, and network topology. OSDs store data; you should decide whether to use SSDs for data, SSDs for journals or WAL with spinning disks for bulk storage, or all-SSD for maximum throughput. The number of OSDs affects throughput and distribution — more OSDs spread load but add management overhead. Placement groups should be sized relative to OSD count to balance distribution and recovery behavior. Network bandwidth is critical: Ceph replication and recovery traffic can saturate links, so provision a dedicated high-bandwidth network, ideally separated into public and cluster networks for client and replication traffic. A concrete example: for an IOPS-sensitive VM pool, use SSD-backed OSDs and a replication factor of three, with a dedicated 10GbE or higher fabric. A common misconception is that Ceph only needs disk capacity; in reality, inadequate network design or too few OSDs will bottleneck performance. Key takeaway: tune OSD hardware, placement groups, and the Ceph network together for the workload profile and test with representative IO patterns before production rollout. Red Hat Ceph Storage Design Considerations means osd hardware, placement group sizing and network bandwidth together determine ceph performance; treat them as a combined design effort.. In practical terms, osds, journals, placement groups, and network bandwidth. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Ceph is a system
keyIdea.text: OSD hardware, placement group sizing and network bandwidth together determine Ceph performance; treat them as a combined design effort.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Ceph Design
Design pillars
OSDs • PGs • Network
OSD hardware
Choose SSD for WAL/journal or data depending on IOPS needs; HDD for capacity pools.
Placement groups
Size PGs to OSD count to ensure even distribution and performant recovery.
Network bandwidth
Provide dedicated public and cluster networks to avoid contention with tenant traffic.
Replication vs Erasure
Use replication for small-block, IOPS-heavy pools; consider erasure for large capacity with less small-write pressure.
Always test with representative IO patterns to validate that OSD choices, placement group counts, and network capacity meet the performance targets for your VM classes.
Scenario card
For a high-IOPS VM pool: 1) Use SSD OSDs or SSD journals, 2) replication factor 3, 3) allocate separate Ceph public and cluster networks at 10GbE or higher, 4) size PGs proportional to OSDs.
Pro tip
Monitor Ceph recovery rates and network utilization during heavy operations; these are early indicators of bottlenecks.

narration.text: Networking design centers on the choice between provider networks and self-service tenant networks. Provider networks map virtual networks directly to the physical infrastructure. They are simple to troubleshoot and deliver predictable performance, making them ideal for external access or high-bandwidth services. Self-service networks are virtual and managed by tenants; they rely on overlay technologies like VXLAN or GRE. They provide isolation and flexibility but add encapsulation overhead and require an appropriately configured underlay. A concrete example: use a provider network for floating IPs and external endpoints to avoid tunnel overhead, and use tenant VXLANs for private tenant segmentation where many isolated networks are needed. VXLAN scales to millions of segments, which is an advantage over VLAN’s 4096 segments, but VXLAN increases complexity in the underlay and requires MTU considerations because of extra headers. A common misconception is that overlays always degrade performance—proper underlay design with sufficient bandwidth and MTU tuning can minimize overhead. Key takeaway: combine both network types: provider networks where physical performance matters and self-service overlays where scale and tenant isolation are primary goals. Provider Networks vs Self‑Service Networks means provider networks for performance and external access; self-service overlays for tenant isolation and large-scale segmentation.. In practical terms, trade-offs: performance and flexibility. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Use both
keyIdea.text: Provider networks for performance and external access; self-service overlays for tenant isolation and large-scale segmentation.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Provider vs Tenant
Provider networks
Direct mapping to physical networks. Use for external access, floating IPs, and services needing predictable performance. Simpler to troubleshoot and avoids encapsulation overhead.
When to choose
High-bandwidth endpoints, external-facing services, and where NIC mapping is required.
Caveat
Limited segmentation count compared to overlays and requires physical VLAN planning.
Self-service (tenant) networks
Virtual networks managed by tenants, typically using overlays such as VXLAN. Provide strong isolation and flexible tenant topologies at scale but introduce encapsulation overhead and underlay requirements.
When to choose
Large multi-tenant clouds needing many isolated segments and tenant-managed networks.
Caveat
Requires underlay MTU and bandwidth tuning to handle encapsulation overhead efficiently.
Concrete example & takeaway
Use a provider network mapped to a physical NIC for floating IPs and public services. Use VXLAN-based tenant networks for internal tenant isolation when you need many segments. Ensure the underlay supports MTU and bandwidth for VXLAN encapsulation. Avoid the misconception that overlays are inherently slow; with proper underlay design they provide scale without unacceptable overhead.

screens.title: TripleO Parameter Choices — Conceptual Example
screens.subtitle: Translate topology choices into TripleO parameters

narration.text: TripleO environment files express your high-level network design choices in parameters that drive the deployment. The conceptual YAML snippet provided in the chapter maps Neutron network type, public interface, and tenant network type to deployment behavior. For example, setting NeutronNetworkType to VXLAN and NeutronPublicInterface to a physical NIC tells the deployment to create overlay tenant networks and map external provider traffic to the chosen interface. Use these parameters to capture decisions such as enabling isolated metadata or choosing tunnel types. A concrete example: setting NeutronTenantNetworkType to VXLAN and defining an ExternalNet with a CIDR and allocation pools provides a repeatable template for the pilot environment. A common misunderstanding is treating these variables as purely operational knobs; they are design artifacts and should be reviewed by networking and security teams. Key takeaway: keep your environment files as design documentation as well as deployment input, and validate changes in a test deployment before applying them to production. TripleO Parameter Choices — Conceptual Example means tripleo parameters encode networking and design choices and should be treated as part of your architecture documentation.. In practical terms, translate topology choices into tripleo parameters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Parameters map choices
keyIdea.text: TripleO parameters encode networking and design choices and should be treated as part of your architecture documentation.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › TripleO Parameters
Conceptual code example
# Conceptual representation (not executable)
parameter_defaults:
  NeutronPublicInterface: 'nic1'    # Physical interface for external connectivity
  NeutronNetworkType: 'vxlan'       # Or 'vlan'
  NeutronTunnelTypes: 'vxlan'
  NeutronEnableIsolatedMetadata: true
  NeutronTenantNetworkType: 'vxlan'

  ExternalNet:
    cidr: '172.16.1.0/24'
    gateway: '172.16.1.1'
    allocation_pools: [{'start': '172.16.1.100', 'end': '172.16.1.200'}]

  TenantNet1:
    cidr: '192.168.10.0/24'
    gateway: '192.168.10.1'
    allocation_pools: [{'start': '192.168.10.10', 'end': '192.168.10.254'}]
Explanation
These parameters record network mapping and encapsulation choices which define how TripleO will configure the underlay and Neutron. Treat them as part of your design artifact set and validate with a test deployment.
Misconception
These values are not purely operational flags; they encode design decisions that impact scale and security and should be agreed by cross-functional teams.

screens.title: Network Traffic Segregation and Interfaces
screens.subtitle: Separate management, API, storage, and tenant data paths

narration.text: A robust OpenStack design clearly separates traffic types across dedicated interfaces and VLANs. Typical traffic categories are management (for orchestration and node control), A P I (service endpoints), storage (Ceph replication and client traffic), and tenant data (VM traffic). Assign dedicated NICs or VLANs for each traffic class to improve performance and limit blast radius in case of failures. For example, Ceph should have its own high-bandwidth network so replication and recovery do not interfere with tenant traffic. Management and A P I networks should be isolated to protect control plane operations and to reduce noisy neighbor effects on tenant workloads. A practical design step is to map each network role to physical interfaces in your environment file and verify MTU settings for overlay use. A common misconception is that a single physical NIC with VLANs is always sufficient; in heavy-load environments separate physical NICs and switching paths may be required to meet throughput and isolation goals. Key takeaway: plan interfaces and underlay capacity with the expected peak behaviors of each traffic class, and validate with traffic-generation tests. Network Traffic Segregation and Interfaces means map management, api, storage, and tenant data to dedicated interfaces or vlans to protect performance and security.. In practical terms, separate management, api, storage, and tenant data paths. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Segregate traffic
keyIdea.text: Map management, API, storage, and tenant data to dedicated interfaces or VLANs to protect performance and security.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Traffic Segregation
Traffic roles
  • Management — orchestration, provisioning and node control.
  • API — service endpoints like Keystone, Nova, Neutron APIs.
  • Storage — Ceph public and cluster replication traffic.
  • Tenant data — VM east-west and north-south traffic.
Map each role to dedicated NICs or VLANs and set MTU for overlays. If tenant overlays are used, ensure the underlay provides sufficient MTU headroom.
Scenario
For a mid-size cloud, provide at least two 10GbE NICs: one for tenant and provider networks, another dedicated for Ceph replication and management. Validate with concurrent load tests to ensure no cross-traffic interference.
Common misconception
Assuming VLAN tagging on one NIC is equivalent to separate physical paths under all loads. It may be acceptable in small deployments but not under heavy Ceph or migration traffic.

screens.title: Security Zones and Service Segmentation
screens.subtitle: Define trust boundaries for control plane, storage, and tenant workloads

narration.text: Security zones group services and networks by trust and sensitivity. At minimum, define a management zone for the control plane (Keystone, Nova A P I, Neutron A P I), a storage zone for Ceph, and one or more tenant zones for user workloads. The control plane should be highly restricted and isolated from tenant data networks. Use security groups and Neutron policies to enforce microsegmentation inside tenant networks, and apply firewall rules at the physical layer for ingress control. Integrate Keystone with enterprise identity providers such as LDAP or IdM for centralized authentication and role mapping; this supports least-privilege access across the cloud. A concrete example: place A P I endpoints and admin consoles on a management VLAN accessible only to operator subnets, while tenant VMs remain on isolated overlay networks. A common error is leaving management endpoints reachable from tenant networks, which increases attack surface. Key takeaway: design zones to minimize lateral movement, map components to zones early, and document the policy so deployment tools like TripleO can enforce them consistently. Security Zones and Service Segmentation means use zones and identity integration to limit access and restrict lateral movement across your openstack deployment.. In practical terms, define trust boundaries for control plane, storage, and tenant workloads. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Least privilege
keyIdea.text: Use zones and identity integration to limit access and restrict lateral movement across your OpenStack deployment.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Security Zones
Zone examples
  • Management zone — controllers, admin APIs, and orchestration services. Highly restricted.
  • Storage zone — Ceph public/cluster networks isolated from tenant traffic.
  • Tenant zones — isolated overlays or VLANs with security groups for workload-level controls.
Integrate Keystone with centralized identity to enforce role-based access and record which users and services may interact with control plane endpoints. Document and map these zone rules as part of your design artifacts.
Concrete policy example
Allow API access only from operator subnets; allow Ceph replication only on the cluster network; restrict tenant-to-management traffic via firewall rules at the leaf switches.
Common mistake
Exposing management APIs to tenant networks for convenience during deployment. This weakens your security posture and should be avoided.

screens.title: Designing a Basic OpenStack Network Topology
screens.subtitle: From requirements to a deployable sketch

narration.text: When designing a network topology, start with requirements: which VMs need external access, which need isolation, expected traffic volumes, and available physical interfaces. Then pick your components: provider network for external floating IPs, tenant overlay networks for isolation, and a router to enable NAT or routed external access. Create a simple deployable sketch: physical switch → provider network mapped to a physical NIC → Neutron router connecting tenant network to provider network → VM with floating IP access. For example, choose a 172.16.1.0/24 external network for floating IPs and a 192.168.10.0/24 tenant subnet. Plan allocation pools and gateway addresses. A common misconception is assuming NAT alone handles security; NAT does not replace proper zone segmentation and security groups. Key takeaway: a concise topology sketch that lists IP ranges, interface mappings, and router connections is sufficient to turn design into TripleO parameters and deployment artifacts. Validate the sketch by walking through a VM's packet path from VM to internet to ensure no unintended paths exist. Designing a Basic OpenStack Network Topology means translate requirements into a topology sketch with interface mappings, subnets, and router connections to produce deployment parameters.. In practical terms, from requirements to a deployable sketch. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Sketch to deploy
keyIdea.text: Translate requirements into a topology sketch with interface mappings, subnets, and router connections to produce deployment parameters.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Network Topology
Topology checklist
  • Define external (provider) network CIDR and allocation pools.
  • Define tenant subnet CIDRs and gateways.
  • Map provider network to a physical interface for external connectivity.
  • Specify a Neutron router to connect tenant networks to the external network.
Example ranges: External 172.16.1.0/24 with gateway .1 and allocation pool .100-.200; Tenant 192.168.10.0/24 with gateway .1 and allocation pool .10-.254.
Concrete example
A VM in the tenant network requests a floating IP from the allocation pool; the Neutron router performs SNAT for outbound connections or routes traffic to the provider network depending on configuration. Verify that firewall rules and security groups allow intended flows.
Why this matters
A clear topology prevents ambiguous interface mappings and ensures consistent deployment via TripleO environment parameters.

screens.title: VLAN vs VXLAN: Capacity and Overhead
screens.subtitle: When to use each encapsulation method

narration.text: VLAN and VXLAN offer different trade-offs. VLAN is a layer 2 segmentation method limited to 4096 segments because of its 12-bit ID. It has low encapsulation overhead and maps naturally to physical switch constructs, making it suitable when the number of segments is modest and physical VLAN management is acceptable. VXLAN uses a 24-bit segment ID and scales to millions of virtual segments, which is crucial for large multi-tenant clouds. VXLAN requires encapsulation which adds header overhead and requires the underlay to handle increased MTU or fragmentation. A concrete example: if you run a regional cloud with thousands of tenants each requiring isolation, VXLAN enables that scale. If you run a smaller deployment with strict physical isolation needs and predictable VLAN usage, VLAN may be simpler. A common misconception is that VXLAN always requires complex SDN controllers; in many OpenStack deployments VXLAN can be implemented with simple overlay configurations, but you must validate MTU and underlay capacity. Key takeaway: choose VLAN for simplicity and predictable performance at small scale, and VXLAN for large-scale tenant segmentation while investing in underlay tuning.

keyIdea.title: Scale vs simplicity
keyIdea.text: Choose VLAN for limited segment counts and simple underlays; choose VXLAN where segment scale demands it and the underlay can support encapsulation.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › VLAN vs VXLAN
VLAN
Low overhead layer 2 segmentation with a 4096 segment limit. Best for smaller deployments or where physical VLAN control is desired.
Pros: Low overhead, simple mapping to physical switches. Cons: limited segment count, physical VLAN management.
VXLAN
Overlay encapsulation with 24-bit segment IDs allowing millions of segments. Good for large multi-tenant clouds but requires MTU and underlay capacity planning.
Pros: Massive scale, tenant isolation. Cons: encapsulation overhead, underlay requirements.
Decision guidance
Use VLAN when segment count is small and physical mapping is acceptable. Use VXLAN when you need large-scale segmentation for tenants. Always validate MTU and bandwidth in the underlay when using VXLAN.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Validation Steps
screens.subtitle: How to avoid under-provisioning and security oversights

narration.text: Architectural mistakes often stem from assumptions that are not validated. Common errors include underestimating control plane resource needs, sizing storage only for capacity and not for IOPS or throughput, and using VLAN-only designs when tenant scale demands overlays. Another frequent oversight is inadequate network segregation for Ceph traffic, leading to replication contention with tenant flows. To validate your design, run a small pilot that includes representative VM classes, stress the control plane with A P I and scheduling loads, and exercise Ceph replication under simulated failures. Record metrics and confirm headroom for peak operations like migrations and backups. A concrete validation step is to deploy a test tenant, run an IO benchmark against a Ceph-backed Cinder volume while simultaneously running create/delete VM operations, and observe latency and scheduler behavior. Misconception to avoid: believing that a successful functional deployment equals a correctly scaled deployment. Functional correctness does not guarantee performance at scale. Key takeaway: incorporate validation tests into your design cycle and adjust hardware and configuration before large-scale rollout. Common Mistakes and Validation Steps means use pilot tests and representative workloads to catch under-provisioning and network design errors before production deployment.. In practical terms, how to avoid under-provisioning and security oversights. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Validate early
keyIdea.text: Use pilot tests and representative workloads to catch under-provisioning and network design errors before production deployment.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Validation & Mistakes
Top mistakes
  • Not reserving control plane resources.
  • Sizing storage only for capacity, ignoring IOPS and network impact.
  • Using a single NIC for Ceph and tenant traffic under heavy load.
  • Exposing management APIs to tenant networks.
Validation checklist
  1. Deploy a pilot with representative VM classes.
  2. Run I/O benchmarks against Ceph-backed volumes.
  3. Simulate node failures and observe recovery behavior.
  4. Measure API latency and scheduler responsiveness under load.
Key Takeaway
Validation reveals hidden scale and performance issues so you can tune design choices before production rollout.

narration.text: Here are the most important concepts to carry forward. First, sizing: always estimate C P U, R A M, IOPS, and capacity, and reserve separate resources for the control plane. Second, provider networks: map to physical infrastructure when you need predictable performance and simpler troubleshooting. Third, self-service (tenant) networks: implement overlays such as VXLAN when you need scale and tenant isolation. Each concept guides a concrete design choice and affects performance, manageability, and scale. When you review a design, verify that these concepts are explicitly addressed and validated through testing. Think of them as short checks during design review: have you sized the control plane, chosen the right network type for each role, and matched storage design to workload profiles? That practice prevents common failures later. Carry these core ideas into your architecture sketch and lab validation work.

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Satisfy sizing, network mapping, and storage-performance needs and validate them with tests.

content.html:

Sizing
Estimate compute, storage, and network resources and include control plane reserves.
Provider Networks
Networks mapped to physical infrastructure for performance and simplicity.
Self-Service Networks
Virtual, tenant-managed networks typically implemented with overlay encapsulation.
Summary
Address these concepts explicitly in your architecture sketch and validate with pilot tests to ensure performance and isolation requirements are met.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 2
screens.subtitle: Storage, encapsulation, and security in one line each

narration.text: Finish with three more compact concepts you should recall. Red Hat Ceph Storage is the recommended enterprise backend for many RHOSP deployments; design it for IOPS, placement groups, and separate networks. VXLAN provides massive network segmentation scale useful in multi-tenant environments; remember to plan the underlay for MTU and bandwidth. Security zones ensure that control plane, storage, and tenant workloads are isolated according to trust levels; integrate Keystone with enterprise identity and apply least-privilege to avoid exposing management services to tenant networks. These concise reminders help you during design reviews and when creating TripleO environment files.
